content.text:
This is squarely in scope, so let me give you the lay of the land — though "cost" splits into a few distinct buckets, which is usually where people get tripped up.

For fine-tuning an open Llama-class model, the cost depends heavily on *which* method you use:

Full fine-tuning (updating all weights) is the expensive end. For a 7B–8B model you're renting multiple high-memory GPUs (A100/H100 class) for hours to days. For a 70B model it balloons — you need a multi-GPU node and serious memory.

LoRA / QLoRA (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) is what most people actually use, and it's dramatically cheaper. You can fine-tune a 7B model on a single consumer or mid-tier cloud GPU. A small QLoRA run can genuinely cost single-digit to low-tens of dollars in compute.

Let me pull current GPU rental rates so I'm not quoting stale numbers.

input.query: cloud GPU rental price per hour A100 H100 2024

content.text:
The numbers back up the ranges nicely. Here's the grounded picture:

GPU rental rates right now: H100 runs roughly $2–4/hr on-demand from major clouds, with spot/budget providers as low as ~$1.40/hr. A100 is cheaper, around $1.50–2.80/hr.

QLoRA on a small model (7B–8B): genuinely a $5–$20 experiment. One commonly-cited tutorial fine-tunes Llama 2 7B on a single mid-tier GPU using spot pricing for "a few dollars." Multiple 2026 sources put a small 7B QLoRA run at under $10.

Full fine-tuning of a 7B model: a different universe — one team was quoted $50,000 in H100 time for a full fine-tune (vs. ~$1,500 doing QLoRA on a single 4090). The full-weight approach needs many GPUs for longer, so it scales badly.

Bigger models (30B–70B): QLoRA still works but the clock runs longer — community reports of ~150 GPU-hours for a 30B and ~280 for a 65B. At ~$2/hr that's roughly $300–$600 per run.

So the honest one-line answer: with QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model is a coffee-money experiment; full fine-tuning or large models pushes you into hundreds-to-tens-of-thousands depending on scale.

One thing worth flagging though — raw training cost is only half the cost story. The piece people consistently underestimate is the *recurring* cost: once you've fine-tuned, you have to host and serve that model yourself (GPU running continuously), versus RAG where your main ongoing cost is API calls plus a vector store. That ongoing serving cost often dominates the one-time training cost over a model's lifetime.

Want me to break down that training-vs-serving (one-time vs recurring) split, since that's usually the more decision-relevant comparison?
